article.overview: A long-period seismometer is a seismometer tuned to slow ground motion: vibrations that repeat over tens of seconds or longer. There is no formal boundary for the term; each instrument is defined by its own published response. The Apollo long-period (LP) sensors had resonant periods of about 15 seconds and a published band from about 0.004 Hz to 2 Hz [1][2]. On the Moon, long-period sensors record the low-frequency energy of deep moonquakes, slow ground tilts and tidal deformation, and the low-frequency background of seismic noise [1][3][5]. Apollo's Passive Seismic Experiment (PSE) carried three matched long-period sensors: one vertical (LPZ) and two horizontal (LPX and LPY) [1][2]. Apollo 14 is the flight documented in the primary report used here [2]. Later designs have broadband or very-broadband responses that extend into the long-period range: the Very Broadband (VBB) sensor of NASA's Farside Seismic Suite (FSS) [3][4], the broadband channel of China's Chang'e-7 seismograph [5] and the broadband sensor of NASA's LEMS-A3 station [8][10]. As of this article's research date (12 November 2026), none of these later designs has been confirmed operating on the Moon. The VBB sensor flew on NASA's InSight mission to Mars [3][6].
article.description:
A seismometer measures how the ground moves. A long-period seismometer is built so that its mechanical response is useful for slow motions. Its main sensing element is a proof mass suspended from a frame by a spring. The mass has a natural (resonant) period, which for the Apollo LP vertical sensor was about 15 seconds [1][2]. Ground motion close to and faster than this period is measured directly; very slow motion is recovered only if the feedback and electronics are designed for it. Long-period sensors are therefore defined by their response curves, not by a single hardware feature.

The Apollo LP sensors were pendulums: the vertical (Z) axis used a LaCoste-type spring, and the horizontal (X and Y) axes used a swinging-gate suspension. Motion was measured with capacitor-type displacement transducers and stabilised by feedback circuits. The feedback could be switched between a flat-response mode and a peaked-response mode [1][2].

Later designs apply the same idea in more compact hardware. The FSS VBB is an InSight flight spare, rotated to measure only the vertical component [3][4]. The Chang'e-7 broadband channel is a three-axis spring-mass sensor with capacitive displacement sensing and negative feedback, with a design band from 1/120 Hz to 10 Hz [5]. A secondary comparison table gives the LEMS-A3 broadband channel as 0.001 to 1 Hz [10]. These figures are design or secondary-source bands, not measured in-flight responses.

A long-period sensor is usually combined with a higher-frequency sensor, because very slow and fast motion need different designs. Each Apollo PSE included one single-axis short-period vertical sensor alongside its three LP sensors [1][2]. The FSS combines its VBB with a three-axis short-period sensor [3][4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
Long-period seismometers serve several connected goals on the Moon:

- **Deep moonquakes.** The Chang'e-7 calibration paper, summarising lunar seismic signal properties, states that the energy of deep and shallow moonquakes is concentrated in roughly 0.01–1 Hz [5]. That range lies within the 0.004–2 Hz band for which the Apollo LP sensors were specified [2], so the LP channel is the natural tool for these events.
- **Tides and tilts.** The Apollo LP tidal mode outputs the unfiltered, unamplified feedback signal, which gives tidal tilts and changes in the magnitude of gravity [1]. The Apollo 14 PSR states that the instrument is also capable of measuring tilts of the lunar surface [2].
- **Background noise and micrometeoroid flux.** The FSS plan was to record about four months of lunar background seismic noise, which is modelled as driven by micrometeoroid impacts, in order to estimate the current impact rate [3].
- **Deep structure and crustal layering.** The first two FSS science objectives are deep lunar structure, including the difference between near-side and farside activity, and crustal thickness and layering, using receiver functions and autocorrelation of ambient noise and coda [3].
- **Artificial impacts.** The Apollo 14 PSR presents LP traces (LPX, LPY and LPZ) from deliberate impacts of the Saturn S-IVB stage and the Lunar Module ascent stage [2].
article.operating_principle:
Like other seismometers, the long-period sensor relies on inertia. A proof mass is suspended inside a frame. When the ground moves, the frame moves with it while the mass tends to stay still. The instrument measures the relative motion between mass and frame. The natural period of the Apollo LP pendulums was about 15 seconds, corresponding to a natural frequency of about 0.067 Hz (1/15 Hz) [1][2].

**Apollo LP suspension and transduction.** The LPZ sensor used a LaCoste-type spring. The LPX and LPY sensors used a swinging-gate arrangement. Because the displacement transducers are capacitive, the electrical output is proportional to the relative displacement between mass and frame [1]. The response model in the Yamada document uses a damping constant h = 0.85 for the LP sensor [1].

**Flat and peaked modes.** In the flat-response mode, the LP sensors have natural periods of 15 seconds. In the peaked-response mode, the feedback filter is bypassed and the transfer function is sharply peaked at about 2.2 seconds [1][2]. The Apollo 14 PSR states that peaked mode increases maximum sensitivity by a factor of 6 but reduces sensitivity to low-frequency signals [2]. The FSS team describes the Apollo LP peaked sensitivity as being near 0.5 Hz, consistent with a period of about 2 seconds [3].

**Tidal mode.** A separate tidal mode outputs the unfiltered and unamplified feedback signal, with the effects of the output amplifier and filters removed [1].

**Leveling and tilt.** The LP horizontal sensors are very sensitive to tilt and must be levelled to high accuracy. The Apollo PSE used a two-axis, motor-driven gimbal for levelling, and a third motor adjusted the LPZ sensor [2].

**Digitisation.** The Apollo PSE recorded data as a 10-bit digital word. One digital unit (DU) is the signal change corresponding to one least-significant bit [2]. The sampling rate of the LP channels is not stated in the sources consulted.

**Later designs.** The Chang'e-7 broadband channel uses a spring-mass system with capacitive displacement sensing, negative feedback to extend bandwidth and range, and an internal electrical calibration coil [5]. The FSS VBB is a flight spare of the InSight vertical VBB sensor [3][4].
article.scientific_importance:
Long-period data matter because the energy of deep and shallow moonquakes is concentrated at low frequency. The Chang'e-7 paper gives roughly 0.01–1 Hz as the band where this energy lies [5]. The Apollo LP sensors covered the lower part of this range, down to about 0.004 Hz [2].

The Apollo LP peak sensitivity near 0.5 Hz is the reference point for later vertical sensors. The FSS team states that its VBB 'should be' about three times more sensitive than the Apollo instrumentation near that peak, and more than an order of magnitude more sensitive away from it [3]. These are expectations stated before the instrument reached the Moon, not measured performance.

Tide and tilt measurements provide a second use for the same channel: the Apollo tidal mode gives tidal tilts and gravity changes [1][2]. Long-period records of artificial impacts, such as the S-IVB and Lunar Module ascent-stage impacts on Apollo 14, also serve as calibration and propagation references [2].

As far as the sources consulted show, the Apollo PSE long-period records are the only lunar long-period data with instrument-level specifications in primary documents. Later long-period and broadband sensors have been specified, but the sources read here do not report their on-Moon measurements.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a long-period seismometer. Each example below describes a specific instrument and states whether it has flown, is flight-proven heritage from another mission, is a design requirement, or is a secondary-source value. Where a value applies to a whole instrument package rather than to the long-period sensor alone, this is stated. Values that are not publicly specified in the sources consulted are recorded as null. The examples use different technologies and different units (velocity, acceleration and displacement responses), so their numbers should not be compared directly.

examples.name: Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment long-period sensors (LPZ, LPX, LPY)
examples.type: Historical lunar instrument (flown and operated on the Moon, Apollo ALSEP PSE)
examples.status: Flown on the Apollo Passive Seismic Experiment. The Apollo 14 instrument is documented in the NASA preliminary science report [2]. The same PSE design flew on other ALSEP stations; those deployments are noted in the companion short-period article and were not re-verified in this run.
examples.sensor_configuration: Three matched long-period seismometers aligned orthogonally: one vertical (LPZ) and two horizontal (LPX, LPY). The PSE also includes a single-axis short-period vertical sensor [1][2].
examples.transducer: Pendulums with capacitor-type displacement transducers and feedback. LPZ uses a LaCoste-type spring; LPX and LPY use a swinging-gate suspension [1].
examples.detection_threshold: Not stated for the LP sensors alone in the sources consulted. The Apollo 14 PSR gives a 0.3 nm detection figure for the PSE 'at maximum sensitivity' and for the SP sensor at 1 Hz, but the subject of the first statement is ambiguous in the extracted text, so it is not used here [2].
examples.package_mass_note: Whole PSE including electronics module and thermal insulation; not the LP sensors alone [1].

station_performance.Apollo 14: LPZ unstable in flat-response mode for reasons not determined; circumvented by removing the feedback filter and operating all three LP sensors in peaked mode. Gimbal motor for the LPY sensor showed intermittent malfunction [2].

examples.description: The Apollo PSE long-period sensors are the only flown long-period seismometers covered in this article. Each PSE contained three matched LP pendulums. Flat-response mode gives a 15-second natural period; peaked-response mode gives 2.2 seconds, a factor-of-six increase in maximum sensitivity with reduced sensitivity to low frequencies [1][2]. The published LP band is 0.004–2 Hz [2]. The PSE package was about 11.5 kg and 23 cm by 29 cm without insulation, drawing 4.3–7.4 W, but these values apply to the whole PSE, not to the LP sensors alone [1]. The LP sampling rate is not stated in the sources consulted.

examples.name: Farside Seismic Suite (FSS) Very Broadband (VBB) seismometer
examples.type: Flight-proven InSight heritage sensor; flight spare planned for the Moon
examples.status: Flight-proven through the InSight mission to Mars; the FSS flight unit was planned for a lunar launch, with the 2024 LPSC update placing the lander's launch in 2026 and a CNES project page listing an in-development status with a June 2026 launch [3][4][7]. No FSS launch or lunar operation is confirmed in the sources consulted.
examples.sensor_configuration: Single vertical axis. The VBB is the InSight flight spare, rotated to measure only the vertical component of motion [3][4].
examples.transducer: Not described in the consulted abstracts beyond its InSight heritage; CNES provided the sensor and IPGP provided design work [4].
examples.detection_threshold: Not stated in the consulted abstracts. The abstracts describe the VBB as capable of measuring accelerations of a few tenths of a nm/s² [3].
examples.package_mass_note: Not stated in the consulted primary sources; a search-result summary of a CNES/NASA page gave a complete-suite figure that was not verified and is not used here.

station_performance.Design claim: The VBB 'should be' about three times more sensitive than the Apollo instrumentation near its peak at about 0.5 Hz and more than an order of magnitude more sensitive away from that peak [3]. This is an expectation, not a measured result.

examples.description: The FSS VBB is described as the most sensitive flight-ready seismometer ever built, a claim the FSS team attributes to InSight heritage [3][4]. Its stated performance target is measurement of accelerations of a few tenths of a nm/s² [3]. The sensor was planned as one of two FSS instruments: the VBB for the lowest frequencies and a three-axis short-period sensor for higher frequencies [3][4]. The suite's lunar status and specification details were not confirmed in the sources consulted. The VBB's band, noise, mass and power are not stated in the abstracts read [3][4].

examples.name: InSight SEIS Very Broadband (VBB) sensor (Mars heritage)
examples.type: Flight-proven Mars heritage sensor (not a lunar instrument)
examples.status: Flown on NASA's InSight mission to Mars. Its flight-proven status is cited as the basis for the FSS VBB spare [3][4].
examples.sensor_configuration: Vertical very-broadband sensor within the InSight SEIS package, paired with the SEIS short-period sensors [6].
examples.transducer: Not described in the sources consulted beyond the DLR mission-page summary [6].
examples.detection_threshold: Not stated in the sources consulted.
examples.package_mass_note: Not stated in the sources consulted.

station_performance.Mission note: Heritage hardware only; its on-Mars data are not used to characterise any lunar instrument in this article.

examples.description: The InSight VBB is included because it is the hardware heritage of the FSS VBB [3][4]. The DLR mission summary gives the VBB range as 0.01–10 Hz [6]. This band is the mission design of the Mars instrument and is not a measured lunar performance. No InSight VBB image has been verified for this article.

examples.name: Chang'e-7 lunar seismograph — broadband seismometer channel
examples.type: Planned lunar instrument (design requirement and calibration plan)
examples.status: Pre-launch calibration of the Chang'e-7 lunar seismograph is described in the Chinese Journal of Space Science paper [5]. The paper describes the instrument's planned eight-year operation near the lunar south-polar landing region [5]. No launch or lunar operation is confirmed in the sources consulted.
examples.sensor_configuration: Two three-axis sensors (broadband and MEMS), giving six data channels. The broadband seismometer covers the low-frequency end of the combined band [5].
examples.transducer: Spring-mass sensor with capacitive displacement sensing and negative feedback; the paper states that negative feedback is used to improve bandwidth, range and linearity [5]. Calibration uses an internal electrical coil [5].
examples.detection_threshold: Self-noise requirement: no greater than 2.5×10⁻⁹ g/√Hz at 1 Hz [5]. Measurement range: magnitude −4.0 to +3.2 (acceleration 2.5×10⁻⁹ to 2.5×10⁻³ g) [5].

station_performance.Design requirement: Output range ±5 V; sensitivity 2000 ± 60 V/g (derived from the ±5 V output and the 2.5×10⁻³ g upper limit) [5]. These are requirement values, not measurements.

examples.description: The Chang'e-7 broadband channel has a design band of 1/120 Hz to 10 Hz, and the paper combines it with a 1–100 Hz MEMS channel to cover 1/120–100 Hz [5]. Its stated requirements are a self-noise level of no more than 2.5×10⁻⁹ g/√Hz at 1 Hz and a magnitude range from −4.0 to +3.2 [5]. The paper states that deep and shallow moonquake energy lies at 0.01–1 Hz, which is why the broadband channel is specified down to 1/120 Hz [5]. Mass, size and power are not stated in the paper. All values are requirements or calibration targets, not flight measurements.

examples.name: Lunar Environment Monitoring Station (LEMS-A3) broadband seismometer
examples.status: Planned for deployment by Artemis III astronauts near the lunar South Pole, with a mid-2027 target in the SSA abstract [8]. A NASA archive entry lists a 2026 launch date, which conflicts with that target [11]. No deployment is confirmed in the sources consulted.
examples.sensor_configuration: A three-axis short-period seismometer complemented by a three-axis broadband seismometer, plus an instrument platform for digitisation, storage, power, thermal control and communication [8]. Two three-axis sensors are reported to be buried in the regolith [9].
examples.transducer: Not stated in the primary sources consulted.
examples.detection_threshold: Secondary table gives a sensitivity of about 10⁻⁹ m/s² [10]. Not verified against a primary NASA document.
examples.package_mass_note: A secondary table lists a mass near 10 kg for the station; the table does not clearly say whether this refers to the broadband sensor alone, so it is not used as a sensor value [10].

station_performance.Design target: Three-month minimum mission with a two-year baseline; after activation, the station needs no power, thermal, commanding or data support from the lander or crew [8].

examples.description: The LEMS-A3 broadband sensor is described as the complement of a three-axis short-period sensor on the same station [8]. Its band of 0.001–1 Hz comes from a secondary comparison table and has not been verified against a primary NASA document [10]. The station was planned to be buried in regolith, which is expected to improve thermal stability and coupling and to reduce noise [9]. Because the broadband figures are secondary, they should be checked against NASA's LEMS-A3 project documentation before use.

physical_specifications.other_concepts: Yamada's document also describes the Lunar Surface Gravimeter (LSG), a separate instrument that measures acceleration over a range of low frequencies and is catalogued elsewhere in this project as payload 016 (Gravimeter) [1]. Japan's LUNAR-A penetrator seismometers and the Lunar Geophysical Network are not covered here because no long-period specification was verified for them in this run.

status_and_technology_summary.instrument: Apollo PSE LP sensors (LPZ, LPX, LPY)
status_and_technology_summary.status: Flown on Apollo ALSEP PSE (Apollo 14 documented in [2])
status_and_technology_summary.technology: Pendulum with capacitive displacement transducer and feedback

status_and_technology_summary.status: Flight spare; flight-proven as InSight heritage; FSS flight not confirmed
Flown on NASA's InSight mission to Mars (heritage)
Pre-launch calibration described; launch not confirmed in sources
Planned for Artemis III (mid-2027 target; launch date conflicting)

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The Apollo PSE sensor unit (containing all three LP sensors and the SP sensor) is 23 cm in diameter and 29 cm high without insulation [1]. No LP-only dimensions are published in the sources consulted. FSS, Chang'e-7 and LEMS-A3 dimensions are not stated in the sources consulted [3][4][5][8].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The Apollo PSE weighed 11.5 kg including its electronics module and thermal insulation [1]; LP-only mass is not stated. The FSS, Chang'e-7 and LEMS-A3 sensor masses are not stated in the primary sources consulted. A secondary table gives a mass near 10 kg for LEMS, but it is not clear whether this refers to the broadband sensor alone, so it is not used as a sensor value [10].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Apollo PSE drew 4.3–7.4 W in total [1]. The instrument heater is given as 6 W in the Apollo 14 PSR [2] and 2.5 W in the Yamada document [1]; the two values conflict and are both recorded. FSS, Chang'e-7 and LEMS-A3 power figures are not stated in the primary sources consulted, except that FSS is designed to run from its own solar panel and batteries [3].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Thermal control is the main environmental concern documented for the Apollo PSE. The instrument has a heater, a proportional controller and an insulating wrapping of aluminised Mylar. An insulating shroud is spread over the local surface to reduce temperature variations of the surface material and, it is expected, thermally induced tilts [1][2]. The Apollo 14 PSR reports that the maximum instrument temperature exceeded the design set point of 125 °F by about 5 °F [2]. For long-period operation, thermal and tilt stability matter as much as raw sensitivity.

Tilt is the second operational requirement. The LP horizontal sensors must be levelled to high accuracy, and the Apollo system levelled them with a two-axis, motor-driven gimbal [2]. The whole PSE drew 4.3–7.4 W [1]. The sources consulted do not state radiation, vacuum, dust or micrometeoroid tolerances for the Apollo LP sensors.

For the later designs, the FSS was designed to survive the lunar night independently of its lander, using a cube-within-a-cube insulation arrangement, a thermal switch and a mini loop heat pipe to reject heat during the lunar day [3][4]. The FSS communicates only during the day to limit night-time power use [3]. The Chang'e-7 paper lists extreme temperature cycling, radiation, low gravity and vacuum as conditions that may change sensitivity and frequency response over time, and describes an on-surface internal calibration to track such changes [5]. Environmental tolerances for the LEMS-A3 broadband sensor are not stated in the sources consulted.
article.limitations:
- **Band edges.** The Apollo LP band tops out at about 2 Hz, so LP records do not capture the higher-frequency energy of impacts and local events that a short-period sensor resolves [2].
- **Flat versus peaked trade-off.** Peaked-response mode increases maximum sensitivity by a factor of six but reduces sensitivity to low-frequency signals [2]. The mode choice therefore decides which part of the band is best measured.
- **Stability.** In Apollo 14 the LPZ sensor was unstable in flat-response mode for reasons not determined; the fix was to remove the feedback filter [2].
- **Tilt and levelling.** The horizontal LP sensors are very sensitive to tilt and must be levelled accurately. The Apollo 14 gimbal motor for the Y-axis showed intermittent malfunction [2].
- **Thermal tilts.** Surface heating and cooling can tilt the local ground. The Apollo design tried to limit this with an insulating shroud [1][2].
- **Design values, not measurements.** The FSS, Chang'e-7 and LEMS-A3 figures in this article are abstract-level, design or secondary-source values [3][5][8][10]. None is a measured on-Moon performance in the sources consulted.
- **Noise floor.** The FSS team states that measuring the lunar seismic noise floor beyond what the Apollo data allowed would help define future requirements [3]. That is a goal, not a result.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A long-period sensor is a surface payload in every example here. The Apollo PSE was deployed by astronauts as part of an ALSEP station [2]. The FSS was planned for delivery by a commercial lander to Schrödinger Basin and was designed to operate independently after that lander's first lunar day [3][4]. The LEMS-A3 station is planned for deployment by Artemis III astronauts near the lunar South Pole, with its seismometers buried in regolith [8][9]. The Chang'e-7 paper describes a south-polar landing region but does not describe its transport chain [5]. The steps below are sourced where possible; no interface with a specific lander or spacecraft is asserted.
transportation_process: Integration and restraint: the Apollo PSE sensors were clamped for launch and transport by pressurised bellows, and uncaging was performed on command by piercing a connecting line with a small explosive device [2].
Launch and transfer: no long-period-specific launch-environment or transfer specifications are stated in the sources consulted, so these phases are not characterised here.

Landing and delivery: the FSS was to be delivered by a commercial lander and was designed to keep operating after the lander ceased functioning at the end of the first lunar day [3][4]. The Apollo PSE delivery vehicle is not described in the sources consulted.

Deployment: the Apollo 14 PSE was deployed 3 m north of the central station, and the PSR reports no difficulty in deployment [2]. LEMS-A3 seismometers are planned for burial in regolith by Artemis III astronauts [8][9].
Setup and levelling: the Apollo sensors were levelled by a two-axis motor-driven gimbal, with a third motor for the LPZ sensor, and 15 ground commands controlled levelling, gain and calibration [2].

Power, data and thermal interfaces: the Apollo PSE drew 4.3–7.4 W and relied on its insulating shroud [1]. The FSS had its own solar panel and batteries and communicated only during the day, via a relay satellite provided by a commercial vendor [3]. The LEMS-A3 station is reported to need no power, thermal, commanding or data support from the lander or crew after activation [8].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo LP sensors were deployed by astronauts as part of the PSE package, with the sensor unit placed about 3 m north of the central station. Ground operation used 15 commands from Earth for levelling, gain and calibration [2]. The FSS was designed as a self-sufficient package mounted on the lander deck. Its inner cube houses the seismometers, battery, avionics and instrument electronics, and its outer cube supports the solar array, radiator and antenna [4]. The LEMS-A3 seismometers are planned for burial in the regolith. Burial is expected to improve thermal stability, ground coupling and noise reduction [9].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo: the PSE was deployed on the Apollo 14 mission by the astronauts [2]. FSS: planned, with no confirmed deployment in the sources consulted [4][7]. Chang'e-7: planned for the south-polar region [5]. LEMS-A3: planned for Artemis III [8]. In the sources consulted, the only lunar long-period sensors that have been deployed are the Apollo PSE sensors.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with any specific lander, rover or crewed vehicle is asserted. The LPSC 2024 abstract says the FSS was to be carried on a lander provided by a group led by Draper [4]; no interface document was consulted to verify that. A search-result summary named an ispace-US lander for FSS delivery, which was not verified. The LEMS-A3 deployment by Artemis III astronauts [8] is a mission plan, not a verified interface with a specific vehicle. No interface document for an Apollo ALSEP delivery vehicle was consulted.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo PSE long-period sensors produced the lunar long-period record discussed in this article. The Apollo 14 PSR documents their operation and the events they recorded, including signals from deliberate impacts of the S-IVB stage and the Lunar Module ascent stage [2]. The PSR also states that all events detected by the Apollo 12 PSE were detected by the Apollo 14 PSE [2]. The Apollo 14 report documents two operational problems, the LPZ flat-mode instability and the LPY gimbal malfunction, which are practical lessons for later designs [2]. The Apollo LP peak sensitivity near 0.5 Hz is the benchmark that the FSS team uses to describe the expected gain of its VBB [3]. The FSS VBB is a flight spare of the InSight vertical VBB, so its heritage lies in Mars hardware rather than in any lunar flight [3][4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- 'Long-period seismometer' names a class of instruments, not one design. The examples here use different technologies, bands and units, so their numbers are not directly comparable.
- The Apollo LP sampling rate, the LP-only mass, the LP-only dimensions and an LP-specific detection threshold are not stated in the sources consulted.
- The Apollo PSE heater power conflicts between the Apollo 14 PSR [2] and the Yamada document [1]. Both values are recorded.
- The Apollo LP frequency-response figures are published as digital-unit graphs. Numeric curve values were not extracted.
- The FSS VBB's lunar status is unconfirmed. Its band, noise, mass and power were not stated in the consulted abstracts [3][4]. Its sensitivity statements are expectations [3].
- The InSight VBB band (0.01–10 Hz) comes from a DLR mission summary consulted through a search summary [6]. The primary SEIS paper was not accessible in this run.
- The Chang'e-7 values are design requirements and calibration targets [5], not flight measurements. The paper does not state mass, size or power.
- The LEMS-A3 broadband values come from a secondary table [10]. The mission date conflicts between the SSA abstract [8] and a NASA archive entry [11]. Neither the band nor the sensitivity has been verified against a primary NASA document.
- The Nunn et al. (2020) lunar seismology review and the Lognonné et al. (2019) SEIS paper were not accessible in this run. No value is attributed to either.
- Evidence gap: the Apollo LP sampling rate remains open. The companion short-period article's 5 samples-per-second LP figure has not been verified here.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url, source_page_url, source_urls and reference url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Direct image URLs were checked with a range request (HTTP 206, image content type) on 2026-11-12. data_quality_notes: catalogue_id is set to the catalogue payload ID (4), following the convention used for payload 003.
Payload name uses the exact catalogue spelling 'Long-period seismometer'.

Apollo LP sampling rate is not stated in the Yamada document or the Apollo 14 PSR text extracted in this run. The companion short-period article (payload 003) gives an LP sampling rate of about 5 samples per second citing its references [10][7]; that figure was not verified here and should be checked against the Apollo PSR and Apollo Seismometer Responses documents before it is relied on.
Heater power conflict: the Apollo 14 PSR gives a 6-W instrument heater [2]; the Yamada document gives a 2.5-W heater [1]. The article records both and does not resolve the conflict.

Apollo LP detection threshold: the Apollo 14 PSR states '0.3 nm' for the PSE at maximum sensitivity, but the subject of that sentence is not recoverable from the extracted text. It is not used as an LP value.
LP-only mass and dimensions are not stated. The 11.5 kg and 23 cm × 29 cm values apply to the whole PSE, and are recorded that way.

Apollo LP frequency-response curves are published as figures in digital-unit (DU) units. Numeric curve values were not extracted, so no sensitivity value in DU per cm is given beyond the statements in the text.
The Apollo 14 PSR and the Yamada document both state the LP period and mode values; they agree on 15 s (flat) and 2.2 s (peaked) and on the 3-LP-sensor layout.

FSS VBB: band, noise, mass, power and dimensions are not stated in the two LPSC abstracts read [3][4]. A search-result summary gave a 40 cm cube of about 45 kg for the complete suite; this was not verified in a primary document and is not used.

FSS status: the LPSC 2024 abstract planned a 2026 launch and the CNES project page lists a June 2026 launch with an in-development status [4][7]. No launch is confirmed in the sources consulted; the status is stated as unconfirmed.

InSight VBB band (0.01–10 Hz) is taken from the DLR mission page via search-result summary [6]; the primary SEIS paper (Lognonné et al. 2019) was not accessible in this run (access-controlled host) and is not cited for any value.

LEMS-A3 broadband values are from a secondary comparison table in an arXiv preprint [10] and are not verified against NASA's LEMS-A3 documentation. The LEMS deployment date conflicts between the SSA abstract (mid-2027) [8] and a NASA archive entry (2026) [11]; both are shown.

Chang'e-7 values are design requirements and calibration targets in the CJSS paper [5], not measured flight performance. The sensitivity of 2000 V/g is derived from the ±5 V output and the 2.5×10⁻³ g upper limit as the paper does.
Chang'e-7 paper PDF was read as extracted text (pdftotext); Springer (Nunn et al. 2020) and HAL (Lognonné et al. 2019) pages were not accessible in this run, so neither is cited for any value.

Image rights: the Chang'e-7 diagram is a journal figure whose licence was not verified; NASA images are generally public domain under NASA media guidelines; the PIA26300 image is NASA/JPL-Caltech credited. The apollo14 and apollo16 images are the same assets used in the 003 article.

Automated URL check on 2026-11-12: all five direct image assets returned HTTP 206 image/jpeg to a 1 KB range request; full-resolution downloads were not checked. Reference URLs were read through local text extraction for the four PDFs (Yamada, Apollo 14 PSR, CJSS, LPSC 2022 and 2024) and through search-result summaries for the remaining web pages.

The 003 article's output files on disk are named short_period_seismometer_payload_003.md and .json without the _v1 suffix that the progress ledger records. This article follows the ledger naming (_v1). The discrepancy is noted here and was not changed.
